utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today is Tuesday, the 22nd of July, 2008. Good morning to the accused. My best wishes for Mr. Pusic who's been absent for a few of days. Good morning to the Defence counsel, to all the OTP representatives, and of course good morning to you, Witness, and good morning to all the people helping us. We are going to continue with the cross-examination. You have used so far one hour and 39 minutes, Mr. Scott. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, and to all those in and around the courtroom. Just before I begin, Your Honour, just for the record the Prosecution is filing this morning a written objection to some Defence documents tendered through the witness -- in connection with the witness Buntic, and we ran into a bit of a computer glitch, but as soon as that's corrected it will be filed straight away this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Zuzul.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'd like to just go back ever so briefly to just a couple of points from yesterday. Again, just in terms of negotiations, would it be fair to say in your negotiations experience, would it be fair to say that in a situation where people are -- parties may expect a cease-fire or a peace agreement, if you will, to, if I can put it this way, break out at any moment or to be approaching, each side at that moment wants to put as much territory as possible under its boot, so to speak. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think that one could put it that way, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And so it wouldn't surprise you in any particular situation in the Balkan conflict that all sides were engaged in that, would it?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't dare to make such a generalised statement in respect of specific cases. Generally speaking, that is correct but I wouldn't dare confirm that for every specific case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And you were asked some questions at one point about military planning and you were shown some documents which seem to confirm that there was indeed some advanced planning of certain military operations. Isn't it also correct, sir, that that's often the idea behind planning military operation because you don't tell the other side what the plans are?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is only logical and understandable that this should be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now -- and then just touching on -- going back to the presidential transcript that we were in yesterday, I asked you about the decision to remove Mate Boban from the negotiations, from the peace negotiations, as of early -- at least early 1994, and I asked you about that and you said - looking at page 87 of the daily transcript from yesterday - and you said: "But whether anyone made a formal decision about that and who made it, I don't know." But, sir, didn't you see it on the very page of the transcript that I showed you that President Tudjman said in no uncertain terms: I made the decision, it was my decision, I decided. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object. Is he asking to verify what's on the transcript or is he asking to verify what was on Tudjman's mind and intentions? There's a distinction there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Not what was on Tudjman's mind, what Tudjman said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Then the transcript speaks for itself. That's the best evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you have some reason to doubt that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that question addressed to me? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Didn't Tudjman say - and if we need to go to it again, if you want to turn to Exhibit P 07856, which we'll be going back to in a moment in any event, it was in the second binder, binder number 2. The usher we'll need your assistance, please.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember what I said yesterday too, and you're right. President Tudjman uttered the sentence which found its way into the transcript. However, what I said or added in my answer and what I wish to repeat today is that I don't know whether a formal body was supposed to verify or make that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: However, as is generally known, the international community always asked President Tudjman to use his influence in the negotiations. We can see this in the specific case. The international community asked President Tudjman to help and intercede in order to make sure that the Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina were forthcoming and -- in these negotiations. Now, I don't know whether President Tudjman issued this decision or not; this is something that I stressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, what you just said now, isn't that another way of just saying -- recognising that everyone involved, the international community, knew of the direct connection between Tudjman and the Herceg-Bosna leadership? It was no secret, was it? And it was for that very reason that the international community approached Tudjman time after time after time?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In fact -- I know you know and you've testified about some of your dealings with Ambassador Galbraith, Ambassador Galbraith testified that the direct connection and the control by Tudjman of the Herceg-Bosna leadership, I think his exact words were was an open secret bearing on be -- verging on being no secret at all. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That he had a direct connection with the representatives of Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina was no secret, open or otherwise. When they came to -- into Zagreb for meetings, this was reported to the public at large. When international negotiators came to Zagreb, it was always a public matter, no secret at all. Now, when it comes to control that you mentioned, that's a different matter. It is true that President Tudjman had quite an influence over the Croat representatives in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I don't think that it was -- that he even had that sort of informal control at all times. I do recall when President Tudjman, or rather, the HDZ of Croatia nominated -- or let me say supported a candidate from Bosnia-Herzegovina, but that candidate was not ultimately elected. He definitely had influence, but I wouldn't say that he always had control.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Going back to the transcript - and if you can find that, please, now that you have the binder in front of you, binder number 2, 7856 - if you'll go to page 8 of the transcript, please, just again confirming as we began to discuss yesterday, your involvement in this particular meeting. On page 8 this statement is attributed to you. "I might suggest, Mr. President, as Mr. Akmadzic and Mr. Zubak received messages to transmit -- in fact, they're similar to what I said, et cetera ..." And then the conversation turns to Mr. Akmadzic and Mr. Akmadzic says: "I would just like to say a few words, as I assume, Mr. President, that Mr. Granic and Mr. Zuzul have already informed you to some extent about certain matters." Was that the case, that prior to, in fact, this meeting you and Dr. Granic had already briefed President Tudjman on these matters?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There's a reference further down in the part that I just read to you about Mr. Akmadzic where he says: "... we spoke with this delegation of the so-called Croatian council from Sarajevo." Can you briefly, please, tell us the Judges what this Croatian council from Sarajevo was?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian council from Sarajevo was an attempt on the part of a group of Croats living in Sarajevo, some of whom were politically active before, others weren't, to get organized as a sort of parallel representatives of Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina. It seems to me that they never gained the support of the Croat population in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Regardless of the fact that representatives of the international community sometimes received them, they never had any actual influence in the communication with the international community. There may have existed a wish for them to be recognised to a greater extent, but what was also evident was the fact that they in fact represented mostly themselves rather than a population.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, Mr. Zuzul, I don't have time to argue about that with you today, but was Mr. Komsic, a man named Ivo Komsic, part of that group?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, he was. Members of that group changed, but I do believe Mr. Komsic was a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if you'll turn to page 28, sir, I'm going to ask your assistance in the -- it might be difficult, but I would ask for you, please, despite whatever differences that the two of us may have, we need to move fairly quickly today. My time is limited, and I'll try to be as concise as I can and I'll appreciate if you can assist us in doing the same. If you'll go to paragraph -- page 28, please, I just want to indicate here this is another intervention by you. Just to confirm what you said yesterday, if you look at the second paragraph under your name and you report to the group, first the conference -- the conference, and I take it that is the reference to the International Conference on the former Yugoslavia, ICFY; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: "The conference is at its death bed, it is presently frozen if not dying ..." So that process had really run its course, so to speak; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you go to page 33, please, and this is still you speaking. You say on the first paragraph on that page you say: "Silajdzic told me, very openly, that Komsic's proposal was not entirely Komsic's. I mean, that's completely clear, because besides this map, which you have in front of you, these are completely developed documents, evidently done by experts. And Redman," he was the US Special Envoy, I believe, correct, "has indicated that he is very familiar with their content." Now, this is the same Mr. Komsic that you mentioned just a moment ago; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the same gentleman.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what did you know at the time and what did you mean when you said that Komsic's proposal was not entirely Komsic's?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said here, Silajdzic told me this and he was not only familiar with Komsic's proposal but Silajdzic said, it seems to me, that the proposal was agreed upon between Komsic and the Muslim side. I also believe that they had already acquainted Ambassador Redman with the proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In fact, sir, isn't it correct that what Komsic put on the table, so to speak, was what came to be the Washington Agreement?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't exactly remember what it was that Mr. Komsic put on the table, but I wouldn't say that this evolved into the Washington Agreement because there still had to -- there was still a long way of negotiations to pass before the agreement would be reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, again, I don't want to spend too much time on it, but it may not -- Mr. Komsic's proposal may not have been the last word, the final version, but isn't it fair to say that it was the concept put on the table at that time that then after further negotiations evolved into Washington?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object again. The witness indicated that he doesn't remember exactly what Komsic put on the table. Now he's trying to force an answer out of him. He can put to the witness what Komsic put on the table and then he can ask whether it's in concert with the Washington Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I disagree, and Mr. Karnavas knows better. It's not required for cross-examination that I do that. I can put propositions to the witness, he wither knows or he doesn't know. Secondly, I can probe the witness. I don't have to accept the first answer given as the last answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, just to clarify, you heard my question, whether or not it was subject to further negotiations and refinement. I repeat to you again: Wasn't what Komsic put on the table what evolved into and ultimately became Washington?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that because I don't know what Mr. Komsic put on the table at the time. However, as I said, the process of the Washington Agreement took a long time. In my earlier evidence I spoke extensively of the negotiations I had with Mr. Biscevic, with Ambassador Biscevic on behalf of our side, and on the other side there were Mr. Silajdzic and Mr. Komsic. The proposals we discussed at the time originated from our side, in fact, from my side. If one closely follows the course of events, that can in fact be taken as the start of the negotiations leading to the Washington Agreement or the talks Mr. Granic had with Mr. Silajdzic or the talks between Mr. Granic and myself with Ambassador Redman --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir. I want to go on, please --

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- all of that preceded --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm very sorry to interrupt you, but let me ask both of you, please slow down a bit for the sake of the interpreters. I would appreciate it very much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I apologise to you again, Mr. Zuzul, I'm not trying to be discourteous, but again time is quite limited and sometimes -- I have to press forward with particular questions. I wish we had more time, frankly. Let me ask you to go to page 59 of the transcript. At the middle of that page, sir, President Tudjman comes back into the conversation and says this: "Well, Gentlemen, what we have heard about this reversal, in the sense that America would attempt to impose such a solution, is not really anything new for us. Because we have always known that the West was interested - as was evident in the case of Germany - in punishing Serbia, if possible, and forcing us to cooperate with the Muslims." Now, two questions. In the first line where President Tudjman says: "... we have heard about this reversal ..." what reversal is he talking about?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I find it quite difficult to interpret at this time what President Tudjman referred to, the reversal. Perhaps he meant the departure from the Vance-Owen Plan which was topical at the time and going on to the first step which would mean the rapprochement between the Croats and the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, to go next to Exhibit P 10535, which would be in binder number 3, please. Sir, this appears to be an interview -- or, sorry, an account of a speech that was given to -- by President Tudjman around this time. The article is dated the 28th of February, 1994, so it would have been a few days after the meeting transcript that we were looking at a few moments ago, a few days later. Now, if you can scan down the page until you see the heading: "Muslim-Croat union in Bosnia-Herzegovina ..." and it starts off with Mr. Tudjman saying: "Today, for the first time, all the relevant international factors from Europe to the USA have reached the conclusion that the survival of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as it is, is impossible and have recommended to us and in their own way consider it necessary both because of us and because of the world for us to accept a solution according to which the Croat nation in Bosnia-Herzegovina would stay in a union with the Muslims ..." Now, we continue on and I'll put a question to you in a moment. Going over to the next page, top of the next page, there's a paragraph that says: "Therefore, they have recommended to us, insisted and persisted, that we must reach an agreement with the Muslims." Now, when one reads this entire article, including the parts that I just quoted to you, in a consistent -- I put to you consistent with President Tudjman's use of the word "reversal" in the presidential transcript, this agreement, the Washington Agreement, represented a fairly abrupt shift from what had happened previously and President Tudjman viewed this largely as something that had been imposed on Croatia by intense international pressure; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should say that all the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia occurred in the context of the international community. On several occasions I stressed that President Tudjman always took as his goal the position of Croatia within the international community, that's number one; number two, the protection of the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Keeping in mind and taking care of these two matters, the position of Croatia and the second matter where up to that point there was the variant whereby the status of Croats within Bosnia-Herzegovina could be resolved either by making them one of the three republics in Bosnia-Herzegovina or by being recognised clearly in a different manner as one of the three constituent nations, that is, entities, in that sense the Washington Agreement was indeed a turning point or reversal because the position of the Croat people was now going to be resolved through a rapprochement with the Bosniak people and through setting up a federal relationship with the Bosnian -- with the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, sir, I'm waiting for the translation and that's why there seems to be a lapse of silence. Sir, if you go to the top of the third page of the document, please, just to follow on this point, President Tudjman is quoted as saying: "This is yet another historic turning point in the life of the Croatian people and in the drawing of those everlasting lines, in the process of demarcation between the worlds and civilizations in this area." Do you agree with that statement?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do agree that this is a statement that I heard on several occasions from President Tudjman, though it was not only from him that I heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I would like to turn briefly to some maps that resulted from Washington.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can have the usher's assistance, I'm looking first at P 10550, and I'm not really sure how those have been -- they should be in the binders, in the third binder, binder number 3 for the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, these are -- there's a collection of maps here that we're going to look at for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: For the courtroom, for the Judges and for counsel, these are maps that have been prepared based on the so-called same base map of the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the municipalities that the Chamber and others have seen since the beginning of the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, Exhibit P 10550, if you can scan that for a moment, can you confirm that this is a map resulting from the Washington Agreement? Does it look about right to you if you don't recall it in every detail?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the map and the details very well because in the -- I took part throughout the duration of the Vienna negotiations. I can't really confirm every line of it, but I do believe that that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And as a result of this process there were two areas which might be considered Croat majority cantons marked in blue, light blue, on the map, number 2 and number 8. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And two rather large mixed -- I'll call mixed cantons, Croat and Muslim, which are marked in hash marks and numbered 6 and 7. Do you see those?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, if you can recall again - and hopefully we can again do this without needing to pull out a number of other maps - but if you can recall -- sir, can you please confirm to the Judges that contrary -- in quite substantial contrast to the maps resulting from the Vance-Owen Peace Plan that were signed in March 1993, a large part of what had been in the so-called Croat provinces 8 and 10 are now instead in the mixed province of 6 and 7?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I can even try to explain to you why I believe that this came to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. Before that I would like to object on the grounds of relevance. Are we prosecuting the Vance-Owen Peace Plan? I mean, what is the relevance of all of this? I think it's an abuse of process to give the Prosecution all this time and then go into areas that are totally not relevant. Where is it in part of the indictment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The Defence so far has put great accent on the fact that the Croatian side accepted the VOPP and always put this to the Chamber as something very legitimate, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It accepted the Washington as well, it accepted the Washington Agreement. It accepted the Cutileiro Agreement, it accepted the Owen-Stoltenberg Agreement. What is this particular line of questioning? What does it have to do with the indictment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think Mr. Scott is the one to answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's why I'm objecting on the grounds of relevance. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Let's listen to Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, this topic, both the Washington and Dayton have been mentioned numerous times by the Defence including with this witness. I think I counted the references to Dayton in this witness's testimony at least 15 references to Dayton in 1995 and at least eight references to the Washington Agreement. So my cross-examination is no different than going into the topics that were raised on direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I beg to differ. There is a difference referencing to the different negotiations that are going on versus prosecuting Vance-Owen Peace Plan with respect -- with what happened at the Washington. I mean, listen to the line of questioning, Your Honours, and I beg you to look at the transcript -- at the indictment and point to me where is it and how is this line of questioning relevant? Now, I don't mind if he wants to spend all that time, but I do think that it is an abuse of process to give the Prosecution that much amount of time simply to harass witnesses. Your Honours, this is pure harassment. It has nothing to do with the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The objection is overruled. Mr. Scott, you may proceed. The Chamber deems that the questions in relation to the Washington Agreement can be relevant in the context.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, if I can next ask you to go in a similar fashion to P 10552, which is a map resulting from the Dayton Agreement. Can you --

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor, certainly but I do wish to mention that I didn't manage to answer your previous question --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I've lost --

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because there was an interruption. If you wish me to answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I do appreciate that, sir. I've lost it on the screen, to be perfectly honest. If we can go back --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: If it helps, Your Honour, page 14, line 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Page 13 --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, sir, here's my question to you, please, and perhaps you recall it, you seem to recall it and I do appreciate your bringing it to my attention. It says: "Hopefully -- but if you can recall, sir, can you please confirm to the Judges that contrary, in quite substantial contrast to the maps resulting from the Vance-Owen Plan that were signed in March 1993, a large part of what had been in the so-called Croat provinces 8 and 10 are now instead in the mixed province of 6 and 7?" And actually your answer was: "Correct." But if you'd like something more, sir, briefly, then please do so.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Croatian side, as is well-known, accepted the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. However, evidently it could not be negotiated fully. Inter alia, the demarcation within zones 6 and 7 could not be negotiated. I often spoke, for example, about the issue of Neum which was very important to the Muslim side, and according to the Vance-Owen Plan and every previous plan it was part of a unit belonging to the Croatian people. The model of the Vance-Owen Plan was the following. There are three entities, both ethnic and territorial. The model of the Washington plan was that Croats enter a federation with the Muslims, and in such a situation the demarcation in the various units in zones 6 and 7 is no longer so important because it was agreed that the Croats and Muslims would hold power together in these areas and that they would not divide the territories according to the ethnic principle. That is why there is this deviation from the Owen-Stoltenberg or the Vance-Owen Plan, which the Croatian side accepted, out of the same desire that it had when it accepted the Vance-Owen Peace Plan and that was to find a solution in Bosnia-Herzegovina that would lead to peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. We're going to have to move forward. If I can ask you to look, please, next briefly at P 10552. And can you just confirm to us, please, that based again on your general knowledge and familiarity with these items, that this is a map which shows the cantons resulting from the Dayton peace process?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's correct, yes, I think that's the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in terms of anything that might be considered Croat majority provinces or cantons, would those correspond with what on this map has been marked as 8 and 10?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to 8 and 10, as a rule, yes. As far as Croatia's concerned there's a big difference in the part marked 2 here, the Bosnian Posavina area. Now the territory marked as Croatian is considerably smaller.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in contrast -- in contrast to that, the total area covered by 8 and 10 in the Dayton map is quite a bit -- significantly larger than the area covered by area 8 or canton 8 in the Washington map; correct? Simply looking at 8 and 10 combined together; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's hard to compare like this. It's probably somewhat bigger, but I can tell you why. In Dayton, in the middle of the negotiations, the principle of percentage of territory was introduced. This was accepted, so the solution of Dayton was sought by establishing the percentage of the territory which would be, so to speak, allocated to or controlled by a particular side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you while we have the map in front of us - and now we'd like to go back to 10550, the Washington map, if you can just flip back for a moment, please. You said during your direct examination testimony that at one point or on two occasions you said Izetbegovic had offered western Herzegovina to Tudjman. Now, at that time how did you define or what did you consider western Herzegovina? What territory was being offered, according to your testimony, to Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I said quite precisely in the course of my testimony that when I was present there was no mention on what territory this was about. That was the situation where I was a witness. In another situation which Minister Granic told me about but where I was not present, Granic told me that then Mr. Izetbegovic mentioned the territory with greater precision. In neither case, to the best of my knowledge, or rather, I'm sure about the first case and according to what Granic said to me in the second also, Tudjman did not take up that conversation, he didn't accept it, so there was no further talk of defining the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you have any reason to agree or disagree that western Herzegovina for these purposes may have been something similar to what is marked on the Washington map as area number 8?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me -- Your Honour, there's answers -- statements being said "no" verbally in the courtroom from the other side of the courtroom. I've heard it now twice. Someone has said "no" twice, I heard it twice. That should not be happening.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Although I am no expert in establishing maps and territories, I'm sufficiently familiar with the area for me to say that this is not a map of western Herzegovina because it does not include areas such as Citluk, such as Capljina, such as Neum. Generally speaking, Herzegovina is a geographic and historical entity which has existed for centuries. It's divided not necessarily by a border, but it's divided into western and eastern Herzegovina primarily by the proportion of the population. In western Herzegovina there were predominantly Croats, Catholics; and in eastern Herzegovina, Orthodox, that is, Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you for that. If I can ask you to go next very briefly to Exhibit P 10481, which should be in the binder number 3, 10481. You find that, sir, and if I can ask you and direct the courtroom's attention to page 10, starting on page 10 of that document. -- or actually, page 9, excuse me. Sir, I just wanted to cover this very briefly because you did mention on your direct examination that you had, in fact, been involved with preparing, I believe, this document at page 27721 of your direct examination testimony you said: "I was present" -- excuse me. "Sometime in mid-June President Tudjman and President Izetbegovic issued a joint statement. I was with President Tudjman when we prepared the statement." So can you just confirm to us that pages 9 and 10 of Exhibit P 10481 is the document that you helped prepare at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'd like to turn next, please, to the topic of President Tudjman's views or positions and connections with Croatia and Croatian territory. You've told us several times that President Tudjman often talked about these matters as an historian, but I'd like to show you in a few moments some statements of people that were dealing with him not as an historian, I put to you, but in an operational capacity, if you will, or in connection with negotiations. Before I do that, you said during your direct examination that one of President Tudjman's motivations or the basis on which he acted throughout this period was in the interest of the Croats living in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that even -- in fact, at one point you said that there was even an obligation under the Croatian constitution to protect the Croats living in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, would you agree with me, sir, however, that doesn't mean - at least in general circumstances - that Croatia would have the right to invade Bosnia-Herzegovina to "protect the Croats" there?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, it absolutely does not mean that, nor am I aware that anyone in Croatia ever even considered such an option or thought of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, let me put to you -- I appreciate that answer but in terms of President Tudjman's stated position as you've described it, a problem with that position, sir, is: Wasn't that exactly Slobodan Milosevic's position in connection with the Serbs, that all the Serbs should be gathered together in one state? And in fact I think that's exactly how you described Greater Serbia when I asked you that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, that's how I described Greater Serbia and that was Slobodan Milosevic's standpoint. However, I never heard President Tudjman express such a standpoint, that all Croats should live in one state, nor did I hear it from any Croatian official ever. I think it would have been treated as absurd had it been uttered.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, I'm just reacting to your testimony when you said repeatedly during direct testimony that Tudjman -- one of Tudjman's principal motivations throughout this period was to act on behalf of -- and in fact that he was under a constitutional obligation to protect the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Doesn't that lead -- that logic lead you to the same position as the position taken by Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all. Those are two drastically different lines of thinking. In many constitutions of democratic countries around the world, there is an obligation to care for the diaspora of that nation or the minority of that nation living in another state. For example, the case of Hungary and Slovakia, the case of Romania and Hungary. There are many states that regulate in this way the fact that it's impossible to organize the world politically in such a way that ethnically pure nations can exist. Europe has abandoned the idea of ethnically pure states long ago. Due to the development of circumstances, a group of Serbian ideologues and Slobodan Milosevic believed that such a model could be restored. However, looking after members of one's nation living in another state cannot in logical or political terms be equated with a desire to take part of the territories of that other state.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir, to look at -- go to, please, Exhibit 8630, P 08630, it should be in binder number 2. And while you're looking for that let me say to you for the record -- I said a moment ago that I would show you some statements from persons who were dealing directly with President Tudjman during this time-period, and one of those persons was Warren Zimmermann, a US ambassador to that region who had extensive dealings with President Tudjman, and I think the Chamber has seen references to his book before. I'd like to ask you about several passages, please. If I can ask you to turn in the preface -- if you can see the numbers at the top of the page, the page -- the preface at Roman numeral IX, the preface at the top of the page of Roman numeral IX, let me just read to you, sir, just bear with me, let me read a couple of passages and I'll ask you a couple of questions about him. About halfway down that page it says: "Franjo Tudjman, elected president of Croatia in 1990, also played a leading role in the destruction of Yugoslavia. A fanatic Croatian nationalist, Tudjman hated Yugoslavia and its multi-ethnic values. He wanted a Croatian state for Croatians, and he was unwilling to guarantee equal rights to the 12 per cent of Croatia's citizens who were Serbs. Tudjman's arrogance in declaring independence without adequate provisions for minority rights gave Milosevic and the Yugoslav Army a pretext for their war of aggression in Croatia in 1991. And Tudjman's greed in seeking to annex Croatian areas of Bosnia prolonged the war and increased the casualties in that ill-starred republic." And if you will then turn to page 75 and then I'll stop and ask you about these. Top of page 75 Ambassador Zimmermann says: "Unlike Milosevic, who was driven by a power, Tudjman betrayed an obsession with Croatian nationalism. His devotion to Croatia was of the most narrow-minded sort and he never showed much understanding of or interest in democratic values. " Now, these words have been written by someone who had extensive dealings with President Tudjman at that time. What is your comment about that?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can make several comments about this. Firstly, at that time I was not active in politics or diplomacy, but I don't believe that President Tudjman, as you said, frequently met Ambassador Zimmermann. They did meet, but not that often. Of course that doesn't mean that Ambassador Zimmermann could not know him very well. On the two pages you quoted there are two different points made. What it says on page 75 about the assessment of Tudjman's personality, we can discuss that until kingdom come, and I don't want to deny that Ambassador Zimmermann or anyone else has the right to hold a certain opinion about someone. Everyone has that right. However, in the first quotation you read Ambassador Zimmermann puts forward his own view of the break-up of Yugoslavia. A time of serious international analysis, including the analysis presented by Ambassador Zimmermann at the time has shown that this interpretation is totally incorrect. In my personal opinion, moreover, in this book which was written at a later date Ambassador Zimmermann is attempting to justify what is now well known.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me take you --

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The catastrophic --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to give you a chance to continue. I'm going to give you a chance to continue. When you're talking about this is Mr. Zimmermann's impressions, let me take you to another part of the book which I put to you he's not stating his impressions, but he at least purports, he at least purports to give an account of a particular meeting with President Tudjman, if you'll go to page 181, page 181, please. And, sir, if you will bear with me and if the Chamber will bear with me on this passage, he describes a meeting in March -- excuse me, in January 1992, on the 14th of January, and Zimmermann says: "Tudjman, as usual, was more bluff in his approach to Bosnia. Among his closest advisers was his defence minister Gojko Susak, a Darth Vader-like individual with black eyebrows and a permanent scowl, whose Canadian fortune had gone into supporting Tudjman's party and, it was believed, buying arms for Croatia. Susak was originally from Herzegovina, and his foremost objective was to wrest the Croatian part of Herzegovina from Bosnia and join it to Croatia. Susak and his ilk relentlessly pressed this agenda on Tudjman, but the Croatian leader didn't need a lot of encouragement." Slowing down for the interpreters. My apology. "In a long meeting with me on January 14, 1992, just a few weeks after his German protectors had bullied the European Community into supporting Bosnia's independence, Tudjman spent over an hour trying to convince me that Bosnia should be split up between Croatia and Serbia. It was the most astonishing single discussion of my years in Yugoslavia. "Tudjman began with a 15-minute monologue. He had just met with a delegation of Croats from Bosnia who told him they felt threatened by Izetbegovic's policies." Now, I would cut through some of this but then I would probably be accused of editorialising so I'll just keep reading. "Tudjman's description of those policies were breath-taking. The Muslims, he said, want to establish an Islamic fundamentalist state. They plan to do this by flooding Bosnia with 500.000 Turks. Izetbegovic has also launched a demographic threat. He has a secret policy to reward regard large families so that in a few years the Muslims will be in a majority in Bosnia (at the time they were 44 per cent). The influence of an Islamic Bosnia will then spread through the Sandzak and Kosovo, et cetera ..." If I might be allowed, skipping down to the next paragraph. "Tudjman admitted that he had discussed these fantasies with Milosevic, the Yugoslav Army leadership and the Bosnian Serbs, and 'they agree that the only solution is to divide up Bosnia between Serbia and Croatia.' Magnanimously, Tudjman said he didn't insist on a 50/50 division ..." et cetera. Skipping to the next paragraph: "Listening to Tudjman I realized I had to abandon diplomatic niceties. With considerable emotion I reminded him, recalling the Iran hostage crisis, that the United States had a lot more experience with Islamic fundamentalism than he did. In our view Izetbegovic was neither a radical fundamentalist nor a threat to anybody. The United States would strongly oppose the break-up of Bosnia. 'Nobody who wants to do this can count on any assistance from us. The threat in Bosnia comes from the Serbs and the JNA not from the Muslims. There will be war in Bosnia if you try to divide it. Don't you think the Muslims will react? What you propose ignores the rights of a large share of Bosnia's population.'" Now, this is described, sir, as a factual account, put forward as a factual account of a conversation and meeting with Tudjman and not Zimmermann's own musings after the fact. Now, do you have any basis to disagree that that's the conversation that Mr. Zimmermann had with Mr. Tudjman on that day?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I think that both you and I and Their Honours certainly know full well the difference between a factual description and a description in a book. Had we before us the minutes of that meeting, and I'm sure that Mr. Zimmermann as a professional diplomat had minutes, then we could talk about a factual representation. These are the impressions of a person writing a book after a lapse of time. I can point to some obvious mistakes quite easily. I think you said in English that Tudjman's monologue lasted about 15 minutes. In the interpretation I heard an hour. Was it correct that you said 15 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I believe that the book says 15 minutes, sir, in that particular aspect -- the monologue portion.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, even the faster of speakers with the clearest of lines of thought wouldn't be capable of saying as much as Mr. Zimmermann says President Tudjman in 15 minutes. You have to take into account that there was interpretation as well and then you see that in that space of time President Tudjman could not have possibly explained all that. How subjective is Mr. Zimmermann in respect of, for instance, Mr. Susak? He speaks of some fortune that Mr. Susak allegedly had in Canada. I must admit that this is something I had never heard either from Mr. Susak or from anyone from Croatia or Canada for that matter. Therefore, he expressed his very, very subjective impressions. The difference between me and the accounts of the books here is that I'm speaking here under an oath, and the authors wrote books for various motives. As for the author of this book, I had the honour of speaking to Mr. Zimmermann and I believe that a motive in his writing the book was to justify the erroneous assessments which he initially made at the start of the break-up of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... I apologise to the interpreters. I know it makes it difficult but I simply don't have time --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is the second time the Prosecutor interrupted this gentleman as he was going into this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, it is and I will continue to do that because of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, then I suggest that he ask more narrower questions. He can't ask a wide-range question and then cut the witness off when he's about to answer the question completely. I think it's unfair to the witness and it's unfair to you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Based on what the witness has said, Your Honour, I would like him to take him to another account by another person that might be differently situated than Mr. Zimmermann, and that is Mate Granic, the foreign -- minister of foreign affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I believe the gentleman is entitled to express the motives of Mr. Zimmermann. If you look at Zimmerman's book --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: He did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I did not cut him off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't wish to debate the point, Your Honours. The point is that the gentleman was not through with his answer and he should be given an opportunity to fully address that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can remember many, many occasions during the Prosecution case when Mr. Karnavas cut off Prosecution witnesses. I regret that my time is limited. If the Chamber would like to expand my time, then I will certainly, in turn, be more generous with the witness. But I think he has answered the question and I need to move forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may speak about this discussion. At page 23, line 1, after a very long question my learned friend, Mr. Prosecutor, ends the question with the following question: [In English] Now these words have been written by someone who had extensive dealings with President Tudjman at the time. What is your comment about this? What is your comment about this. Then the witness starts -- then the witness was -- as soon as the witness mentioned that it seemed that Mr. Zimmermann also issued another book after this one, he was cut off. And then there is -- this is the second round which my dear colleague Karnavas was talking about. So the question was: What is your comment? Unless the witness said: This is my comment, he's still responding. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, in relation to what Mr. Kovacic has said, a minor detail. It looks as though Mr. Zimmermann published a second book after this one. Have you read this second book by him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I spoke of the same book. I read the book, admittedly a long time ago, and I discussed this particular book with Mr. Zimmermann and I expressed my great disagreement with his interpretation of the events. We had this conversation over a lunch in Washington. He had his opinions on the matter, but I wish to stress that these are solely the opinions held by Mr. Zimmermann and not of the state that he represented. What's more, time showed that or proved his opinions wrong. Recently CIA reports were published dating from that period, which showed that the CIA had completely erroneous assessments as to what was going to happen and how the break-up of Yugoslavia -- or completely different assessments of how the break-up of Yugoslavia was going to unfold.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this information. Please proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think we can probably all agree that that probably wasn't the first or the last time that the CIA got something wrong, but be that as it may if we could go, please, to Exhibit P 10402. This is a -- this comes from a book written by Mate Granic, the foreign minister of Croatia during this period and a person who you described at least in part as your immediate superior and a person from whom in addition to President Tudjman directly you took instruction from. There's much in the book that we could cover, again, if we had more time, but I'd like to direct your particular attention, please, to page 71 -- excuse me, my apologies, it should be in binder number 3, P 10402. On page 71 Mr. Granic says -- and he's referring in the context, I represent to you, to the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina, if you look at the previous passages and pages. "As the minister of foreign affairs, I often spoke about the situation there," a reference to Bosnia and Herzegovina, "with Tudjman. Bosnia and Herzegovina was his favourite topic. He always talked about it at the strategic level while he left to Susak all practical issues including military aid, the financing of Croats or political relations with the BH, HDZ. Despite the enormous confidence he had in Susak, I knew that Tudjman occasionally received information from other sources. He was in direct contact with Darinko Bago and often spoke with Zdravko Sancevic, Croatian ambassador in Sarajevo and Ciro Grubisic, the general consul in Mostar who had been appointed at the insistence of Susak. Tudjman's obsession was to recreate the Croatian Banovina which had been established in 1939 based on the Cvetkovic-Macek Agreement according to which Herzegovina and parts of Central Bosnia and Bosnian Posavina were joined to Croatia. The president often told me that Banovina was the best solution." Now, are you suggesting that this is another account that was only simply Dr. Granic's impressions and he had his own agenda here or do you have any reason to disagree that this is an accurate accounting by Mate Granic of his dealings with President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I want to stress first of all that I speak here under an oath, whereas Mr. Granic wrote his book while he was participating in political campaigns. My statements aim at the truth and of course the motives he had for writing this book are probably the motives shared by all politicians when writing their books. It's true that Mr. Granic had very frequent contact with President Tudjman. It is most certainly true that oftentimes they discussed Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is not true that Mr. Granic did not have any political tasks or influence vis-a-vis Bosnia-Herzegovina; quite the contrary, he very often did have tasks as the foreign minister. What's more, the ambassadors reported primarily to him, regardless of their contacts with President Tudjman. I had never heard from President Tudjman or I had never heard President Tudjman say that in territorial terms Croatia should have the borders of the former Croatian Banovina. I tried to show the full extent of the absurdity of that idea on the map we looked at yesterday. I cannot claim or state anything about what Mr. Granic might have heard from anyone including the president. However, to my mind, or rather, he did not speak to me either as an ambassador or as a friend. I still remain a friend of Mr. Granic's despite the fact that we do not belong to the same political parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In terms of the Banovina, you said this several times you said it yesterday, I put to you that what was being discussed here was not to reshape Croatia in its entirety in the form of the Banovina but to take the existing territory of Croatia, the existing territory and borders and add to it those additional parts which were part of the Banovina. Now, that's logically what was being discussed or put forward, isn't it? It was Croatia plus the Banovina, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how you put it. My answer to that is that this is an absurdity. Who could be so naive as to try and restore a solution from -- dating back from history and think that this would involve only gain and not loss? Tudjman was not so naive as to think that he would be able to take the territories which belonged to Banovina while not being aware of the fact that he might lose those parts of the territory that weren't even included in the Banovina ones. Besides, the memories the Croats had -- have of Banovina mostly tend to go in the direction of Serbia. Nowhere was it stated that Tudjman wanted to take those territories that are part of Serbia and which used to be once Banovina. I can tell you that based on my experience which was extensive I never ever believed that anyone in Croatia would consider to expand the borders of Croatia in order to fit in territorial terms the borders of the Croatian Banovina. When Tudjman - and allow me to finish - mentioned the borders of the Croatian Banovina he was referring to the resolution of the national issue between Croats and Serbs. He spoke of specific solutions in terms of organization, and it is true that he went back to that frequently. However, interpreting this in territorial terms is something that I'm fully convinced - and I'm speaking under an oath - is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, let me put it to you, you can tell the Judges that Mr. Tudjman never said those things to you. You can say that it would surprise you to hear those things, that wouldn't fit in your experience. But I put it to you, sir, do you have any basis for saying, were you in the room, were you in all the meetings between Tudjman and Granic, do you have any basis to say that Granic is lying in his book when he says that this is his deal -- these are based on his dealings with Tudjman? Maybe you didn't hear it, but are you saying that Mr. Granic just made up these statements?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the Prosecution could have called Mr. Granic and asked him to repeat or not repeat the assertions he made in his book under an oath here. What I tried to say earlier on --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... are you calling Mr. Granic a liar in making the statements that he makes in his book?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you are using generalisation that I would never use. I wouldn't say that Mr. Granic is a liar. However, what I'm trying to say for the third time now is that if President Tudjman ever told him something along those lines - and I don't know what it was that they discussed - then the only logical and normal thing would be that he should to me as an ambassador and he as a superior and he to me as a friend and I'm still his friend, that he should tell me so because that was important for our work. I'm convinced that neither I nor Mr. Granic would take part in such business, in the business of taking away territory from another state. I'm asserting here that Mr. Granic had never told me that he had had a serious conversation let alone some sort of instructions from President Tudjman about the territories --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir --

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- [indiscernible] another state.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- let's then go, please, to another participant in these events whom we've heard about frequently in this courtroom, not least of which from the Defence side, Lord Owen. If you'll please turn to P 08632 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we move on to that document, Witness, let's remain with this document we have in front of us. The Prosecutor put questions on the part of the text, but there's another part in it that seems relevant. Let me sum it up as follows. Tudjman is alleged to have said to Mr. Granic that in his view the Banovina was the better solution. Granic in his book wrote, and as you view it, in a political context to say this. The idea of dividing Bosnia and Herzegovina into three republics in Granic's view was to say at least in Lord Owen's mind, but also this seems important to me. Tudjman believed that the English and the French wanted to divide Bosnia and Herzegovina but that the division was indeed not possible or only possible if the USA agreed to it. And from what Mr. Granic seems to say, that seems to be the conclusion in this page. He would only have been convinced about this at the beginning of the Washington negotiations. You were in the very heart of all these negotiations. In Tudjman's mind, was his mind somehow maybe influenced by the game played by the British and the French who were not opposed to a division of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but that this would only have been possible with the Americans' agreement. And apparently Tudjman only realized this when the Washington negotiations started and he did not realize that before. What do you think, because this is what Mr. Granic wrote. You were a friend and you may still be a friend of Mr. Granic's. Maybe you discussed the issue with him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I discussed the Washington negotiations particularly extensively with Mr. Granic, and I believe that both of us presented to President Tudjman quite adequately both the position of the international position of Croatia and the fact that the Washington Agreement may lead to a solution acceptable to both the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the international community. It is true that sometimes President Tudjman was under the impression that some representatives of the international community, and perhaps particularly the British, were in favour of a division of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Perhaps the fact that contributed to this most, when we're speaking of an atmosphere surrounding the negotiations, was the meeting between Muslim -- or the agreement between Muslims and Serbs that was brokered by Lord Owen and this agreement allowed the Serb entity to, should they decide so, leave Bosnia-Herzegovina two years later or separate from Bosnia-Herzegovina. I spoke about this at the start of my testimony. I personally believe that President Tudjman would have accepted a division of Bosnia-Herzegovina if such a division had been made by the international community if such a division had -- did not endanger the interests of the Republic of Croatia and if such a division ensured the protection of the rights of Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, I believe that President Tudjman was aware of the fact that these conditions could not be met, and that is why I maintain that he looked for a solution of the issue of Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina within the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I particularly assert this in respect of the period between 1992 and the Dayton Accords when I was actively working on this and had frequent discussions about it with President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Scott, before the break, you had a last document you wanted to submit to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you very much for that. If we could just finish this one document then we could come back to another topic after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you just in your last answer in the last few minutes made subtle references to Lord Owen, and it's to Lord Owen's book that I would like to go next, please, P 08632, which is in binder number 2, 8632, please. This is an excerpt from Balkan Odyssey by David Owen and I would like you to go, please, to page 36. There are two parts to this, it's in one paragraph, but there's two parts that I will read to you but there's two aspects that I'd like to address. On page 36 it says, starting about a quarter of the way down the page perhaps: "Because the 1939 Cvetkovic-Macek Agreement had given the Croatian nation control over substantial parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina many Croats, not least Franjo Tudjman, never in their hearts accepted the 1945 boundary between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina." It mentions -- "similarly, the Serb-inhabited areas ..." and he goes on and talks about that. Skipping down a few lines, everyone has it in front of them. It goes on to say: "This resistance was particularly strongly felt after 1945 for the inhabitants," which had been referred to in part by the Krajina, "the inhabitants had been subjected to genocide by the Croat Ustashas during the Second World War. Very few commentators in 1995 understood or acknowledged that when the Croatian government attacked the Krajina they were not 'retaking' or 'reoccupying' this land, for the Serbs had inhabited it for more than three centuries. At most, the Croats were reclaiming territory." Now, as for the first part of that passage, is it not clear to you, sir, that here again another international, senior international representative, it was very clear to him that Tudjman very much had in mind this view, this implementation of the 1939 agreement or are you saying that Mr. Owen, apparently like Mr. Zimmermann and like Mr. Granic, had just made this up?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, neither in the case of Mr. Zimmermann nor in the case of Mr. Granic did I say that they invented it all. I merely said that those were their very subjective interpretations. One needs not be -- need not be a psychologist or a lawyer to know how different subjective interpretations can be. The passage that you've just read out shows the full complexity of the issue of the Banovina. If you ask me, now that I'm looking at this passage, it can be used for exactly the opposite argument, that's to say that Tudjman would never even attempt to implement the idea of the Banovina because the precise issue that you quoted would be raised, that the Serbs would ask for their territory to be defined within Croatia and that's the last thing that Tudjman would accept. As the vast majority of Croats, I am also convinced that Tudjman believed that the AVNOJ borders of Croatia were the best solution for the Republic of Croatia and that when we're discussing borders it is unjustifiable to rule out the evident fact, which is that the borders of the Banovina leave out vast parts of the Croatian territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And just again, as I said, to finish up on this passage before we take the break, the second part of it, can you confirm, sir, that in fact the area called the Krajina, this was an area of Croatia that had been occupied by the Serbs for, as Mr. Owen says, more than three centuries; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. They reached those areas fleeing the Turkish occupation. That was an area that had been inhabited by Croats for -- by that time for some 12 or 13 centuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And isn't it true, sir, that in fact what you've pointed out several times about this, that it was a contradiction that a number of people, both domestic politicians in Croatia and international representatives, it was a contradiction pointed out to Tudjman on a number of occasions that he could not support Herceg-Bosna on the one hand and deny the claims of the Serbs in Croatia on the other; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor. The international community also accepted the fact that there was a difference in terms of the position of the Serbs in Croatia and the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina. All the documents of the international community and all the results of all the negotiations speak of the Croatian people as one of the three constituent nations in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. All the communications between the Republic of Croatia and the international community about the Serb population in the Republic of Croatia had the intention of providing that population with the highest possible level of rights. I believe that drawing a parallel there is quite wrong. So with the intention of providing the population with the highest possible level of rights as a minority. May I just say this, I will agree with you on one point. Had Tudjman really intended to include a part of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina into the territory of the Republic of Croatia, then there would certainly have been many of those who would have claimed that the same right is enjoyed by Milosevic and his ideologues to include the territory inhabited by Serbs in Croatia into the Republic of Serbia. I do agree that there are many individuals who would have had this line of thinking, and I believe that this is one of the reasons, among others, why President Tudjman never even contemplated the inclusion of parts of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina into the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to have a 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Mr. Scott, you still have two hours and three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I appreciate that, and I'm -- I need to ask -- I'm afraid I'm going to have to ask the Chamber that despite my continued editing down I'm going to ask the Chamber if I could possibly have another hour of time. I think we were -- safely we'll finish this witness I think tomorrow, but I would ask for the Chamber's indulgence. The Defence has had a total of seven -- a bit over, I believe, seven hours with the witness altogether, and I would ask to have some additional time. I need to know that now rather than later so I know how much I have to alter my plan, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I would object on the grounds that time that was given was not used properly. We've gone into areas that were not necessarily relevant, and I think had the time been managed I would be much more gracious in agreeing to more time. But I'm afraid that given what I've seen, that more time would only be wasted.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I also wish to have it put on the record that General Petkovic's Defence objects to the fact that the cross-examination of General Petkovic's Defence is being added to the time that the Defence of Dr. Jadranko Prlic had, and that is -- the witness is his witness. So I feel it is unjustified to add together the times of two Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber will deliberate on this matter later. Please proceed for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just to respond ever so briefly. I'll of course put myself completely in the Chamber's hands if the Chamber thinks that I've used my time unwisely. I think the matters that we've covered have been all of them been quite relevant and directly pertinent to the case. As to Ms. Alaburic's comments, I mean I have to respond to all the questions put by the Defence to this witness including those put by co-accused. I don't know why it would be the case that that time shouldn't somehow be considered. Other than that, other than that, Your Honour, as I say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a moment. We will confer now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. The Bench's microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, having pondered the matter and listened to your request, having taken into account the objections raised, the Chamber decides to give you an additional 30 minutes. This should allow you to finish today.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm gracious for whatever additional time the Chamber can allow me. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Zuzul, just one point that hopefully we can take fairly quickly. We've talked in the last two days about the parts of Croatia that were occupied, approximately one-third of the country that was occupied by the Serbs in the latter part of 1991, including those parts that then came to be claimed as para-states or autonomous zones, such as the RSK, the Republika Srpska Krajina. Let me just ask you as a senior member of the Croatian government, at any time that those parts of the territory of Croatia were occupied or claimed by the Serbs, did you ever consider that they were not -- that they did not continue to be part of the sovereign territory of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, never at any time or in any situation was it the position of the overall Croatian leadership and President Tudjman; rather, the position was to attempt through negotiations to gain control of the entire territory of Croatia as fortunately happened in Eastern Slavonia. If this was not possible, then the Croatian government and the Croatian people were prepared to restore the territory through military operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you for that, sir. That wasn't exactly my question. My question was a bit -- I think, a little simpler than that. At any time during 1991 until the time that those territories were ultimately restored some years later to the territory of Croatia, did the Croatian government ever consider those territories to cease being territory -- the sovereign territory of Croatia? Did you ever consider: That's not Croatia anymore?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it correct, sir, that that was the case despite the fact that, for instance, in the RSK the RSK had set up its own government, had its own currency, had its own military force, but, nonetheless, you consider that to be -- continued to be throughout that time-period the sovereign territory of Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, going to the so-called Friendship Agreement from July 1992. As I understand your testimony, sir, on the involvement of the Croatian army on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that as it was put to you your position was that the presence and involvement of the Croatian army in Bosnia-Herzegovina during at least 1992 was, I'll say, okay, was not a problem, because the Croatian army there was there by agreement to fight together with the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina against the Serbs? Does that accurately state or summarize your position?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my position was then, as now, that the fact that parts of the Croatian army in early 1992 were there was indispensable to prevent the Serbs from achieving their goals, that is, to defend southern Croatia and also to defend part of Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... sorry, but my time, as you've heard, is very limited. It may have been necessary for them to be there but that didn't give them the right to be there, on the sovereign territory of another nation's state. So put aside whether they needed to be there. You've said that they -- I don't think there's any dispute, if I understand your testimony correctly, that they were there in 1992, and as I understand your justification for that is that it was there by agreement with the Bosnian government in a fight together against the Serbs. That's your justification for the Croatian army being on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, in your previous question, which I'm re-reading, you asked me to summarize my position; and in my response that's what I started to do but you interrupted me in the middle of my response. If you're asking me about my position, I had to say what I said as the first part of my sentence. As the second part of my sentence I would add --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you're going to do this I'm going to interrupt you again, sir. My time is limited. My question is not whether you considered it or others considered it indispensable for Croatia to be in that territory; that does not give them the right to be there. Now, on what legal basis or agreement or consent do you purport that it was okay for the Croatian army to be operating on the sovereign territory of the UN Member State of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, Mr. Prosecutor, you are putting questions in such a way that it's impossible to give you answers as simple as you wish. In your question you say that this was the sovereign territory of a UN Member State, and we are talking about a period when Bosnia and Herzegovina was not yet a member of the United Nations. So we cannot put it all in the same context --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... forward, sir, from May 1992 forward when Bosnia-Herzegovina was admitted to the United Nations as a Member State and its independence was recognised, from that date forward, let's talk about that.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: You put your question about early 1992. --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I've changed it, sir, I've changed it. From May 1992 forward, please answer my question.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even before and certainly from May 1992 onwards, Croatian diplomacy had intensive communications and took steps to reach an agreement with Bosnia-Herzegovina in order for us to achieve our common goals and several agreements were signed to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And one of those agreements, is it correct, then came to be the so-called Friendship Agreement of 21 July 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's completely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, in that regard, if I can ask you, please, to turn to a Defence exhibit but it's in Prosecution binder 3, 1D 02295. Sir, you were shown this exhibit during examination by the Defence. This was a letter from Mr. Abdic to Croatia dated the 6th of August, 1992, asking Croatia's consent to establish an ABiH Main Staff logistical centre or centres in Croatia. Do you see that or do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see it in my binder, but I'll try and look at it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. If we missed it, my apology. If you can look on the screen, please, and my apologies to the Judges and counsel if it's not in the binder, Defence Exhibit 1D 02295. I'm sure it's my error and I take responsibility for it. But, sir, if you look at that document it was shown to you and discussed during your examination, and in fact at page 27736 you said: "I think that Mr. Abdic was referring to the agreement that we had just looked at and discussed," which I will tell you in the transcript was the 21 July agreement. And then you went on to say: "... because this letter is only a logical part of the implementation of this agreement." So would you agree with me that, sir, that this was it was fully appropriate for Mr. Abdic or the Bosnian government to send such a communication in carrying out the Friendship Agreement asking for further specific approvals from the Croatian government in order for the Bosnian government to carry out activities on the sovereign territory of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just to expand on that a bit, if we can take that as an example. Would you agree with me, sir, that the fact that Izetbegovic and Tudjman had signed the 21 July 1992 agreement did not mean that either state was free to move and roam at will and conduct activities on the territory of the other without further -- without further agreements and consent; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's hard to answer such a general question, respond to such a general statement. I think we --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let me explain to you, sir. Let me explain it to you, sir, let me put it in a law enforcement context if you've ever come up in this situation. Countries have agreements to cooperate in law enforcement together. And there may be one between, say, the United States and the United Kingdom. The fact that that agreement exists doesn't mean that law enforcement agents of the United States can freely enter the United Kingdom and roam at will and carry out law enforcement activities on that territory.
