You have to give notice to the local authorities, we're coming here, we appreciate your cooperation, maybe there's a liaison officer who will be working with us, and that's the way these things normally work, correct, and that would have been the same here and that's why Mr. Abdic sought further approval to carry out activities in Croatia and that's what you would expect, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, moving forward, sir, because again our time is quite limited, you don't -- I take it it is not your position or is it that once the war broke out between the Croat and Muslim forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina, it's not your position, is it, that that Friendship Agreement was then the basis for the presence or involvement of the Croatian army on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina for the purpose of fighting against the Muslims; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In your question there are several statements, but I thought and still think that the Friendship Agreement between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina was based on the idea of putting a stop to the conflict between the Croats and the Muslims; that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, again, we don't have time to go through all the documentation on this point and we can't, as the Chamber I'm sure appreciates, we can't put our full case to every witness. But taking -- assuming for the purposes of these questions that the Croatian army was present in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992, 1993, 1994 on the side of the HVO, fighting against the Muslims, the Friendship Agreement would not have been a legal basis excusing their involvement on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, would it?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The parts of the Croatian army which were on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992 - and you said that was the period we were discussing - were fighting primarily the Serb forces, the Serb -- or rather, the Yugoslav Army together with the Muslim forces there --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, let me take you to 1993, please. You know and I'm sure you know that after a skirmish, an open armed conflict between Croats and Muslims in Prozor in October 1992, a further round of serious fighting in January 1993 in Gornji Vakuf and Central Bosnia, and then the major conflict breaking out in mid-April 1993 that continued until at least the end of 1993, there was a major war going on between the Muslim side, the ABiH, and the HVO. And I put it to you, and for purposes of this argument, that during that time from January 1993 until February at least of 1994, the Croatian army was present in Bosnia-Herzegovina on the side of the HVO. Now, if that's the case, are you telling the Chamber that the Friendship Agreement signed in July 1992 made that okay? It was okay to fight against that lawful government because of a Friendship Agreement entered into previously under different conditions?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In your question you include a lot of statements I do not feel confident in commenting on because I'm not aware of most of the events you mention. What I do know and what I repeat is that the agreement signed in July 1992 referred to the situation as it was then, but I also know that throughout 1993 there was communication and diplomatic efforts were made to find a solution for the relations between Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the Republic of Croatia. I have spoken about that extensively and I can say a lot about that because I'm quite familiar with that. As for what happened on the ground, I do know that there were conflicts, of course. I apologise. I knew, of course, there were conflicts, but my knowledge was not nearly so precise for me to be able to testify with the same precision about the events on the ground as I have about the diplomatic efforts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let's talk about another historical example and see -- if we take it out of this particular context it will be easier to come to an understanding. You may recall at the beginning -- at the early part of World War II Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union entered into a non-aggression pact in August 1939. Approximately 22 months later in June 1941 Hitler went back on the non-aggression pact and, in fact, invaded the Soviet Union. Now, I take it is it your position that it was okay for Hitler to invade the Soviet Union based on the fact that 22 months earlier they had entered into a non-aggression pact --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, I think that's a bit far-fetched, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Really?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes. I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't see it myself but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it doesn't really matter. With the greatest of respect this has been going on for quite a while. There has been a ruling by the Trial Chamber. The thoughts of counsel are really not relevant. I think we can just simply move on and accept the finding of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, but I didn't interject any thoughts. I put the question to the witness, and while I understand that Judge Trechsel may disagree with me, I wasn't expressing any thoughts other than putting questions and positions to the witness. But having said that, I'll be happy to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, as a specific example, then, moving forward from World War II, the example that we use concerning Mr. Abdic. Can you think of any examples at the time when in 1993 during the conflict between the Croat forces and the Muslim forces in 19 -- excuse me, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that there was ever a time when the Croatian government asked for consents or permissions for its armed forces to operate in Bosnia-Herzegovina against the forces of the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Can you give me an example of anything where there was a letter to Mr. -- dear President Izetbegovic, pursuant to the Friendship Agreement of 21 July 1992, we hereby seek permission for our armed forces to enter into your country and wage war on your forces. Can you point me to any letter like that?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, you are saying things that are totally absurd and yet you are expecting logical responses from me. I think these are absurd statements. I think it's offensive that you want to suggest that I would draw a parallel between World War II and the agreement between the Nazis and so on and the agreements I achieved in a sincere effort to achieve peace. Each of us has the right to his own dignity and I find this offensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So you're not going to answer my -- you refuse to answer my question then. Do you know of any such agreements or communications to that effect --

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, Mr. Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- no. I'm not refusing to answer questions, but I do refuse to have you offend me directly or indirectly. I will answer every question I know the answer to; that is why I came here quite consciously and of my own free will.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... do you know of any communications between the Croatian government and the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the effect that I put to you a few moments ago?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's been asked and it's been answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, it has not been answered. We've had a speech --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It says: "No" --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- but we haven't had an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- "no, Mr. Prosecutor." "So you refuse to answer my question." He's got his answer to his question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No. He says, I'm refusing [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The question was absurd and he got an answer to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I disagree with Mr. Karnavas's position. If the witness clarifies that his answer was no, he doesn't know of any communications then I accept that. But if his answer is no, I'm refusing to answer -- not answering your questions and then on -- and goes on to make a speech then I don't know the answer to his question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, is it your answer that you do not know, the answer is no, you do not know of any communications between the Croatian government and the Bosnian government authorising the operations of armed forces of the Republic of Croatia on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina to engage in war against the forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina? You either do know of such communications, you don't -- as Mr. Karnavas likes to say, you either know, you don't know, or you don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of such communications that are contained in this extreme example that I termed an absurdity, I am not aware and I don't believe that there were any such communications. That there had been communications all the time between the Government of the Republic of Croatia and the Government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina is something I am certainly aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges, please, what you know about citizens of the Republic of Croatia being forced to fight in Bosnia-Herzegovina against the ABiH involuntarily?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I truly do not know enough about this matter in order to be able to comment upon it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall it being reported in the Croatian press around that time that the families of various Croatian soldiers were protesting their sons being sent to fight in Bosnia-Herzegovina and that criminal charges were brought against some of these young men who would not go and fight in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do seem to recall something about that being written about but at my work-place in Geneva I did not receive such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let me just ask you to quickly look at a couple of things to see if it might jog your memory. If you could please look at P 10547, it should be in binder 3, P 10547. While you're looking for that, sir, I'll just say for the record that this is a report from the United Nations Centre for Human Rights based in Zagreb dated 3 January 1994, reporting the drafting of men in Croatia, in this particular instance of Bosnian origin, to be sent to fight in the country of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Point number 4. "The persons who appealed to the objection of consciousness were beaten in the barracks. "All the drafted were told they would be sent to fight in BiH." It makes reference -- also at the top it says: "We received information from the Committee for Human Rights that Croatian citizens born in BH were mobilised on 15 and 16 December 1993." Now, with that in mind if I can ask you, please, it should be close in the same binder, turn to P 10555. I suggest to you that this is the referenced report from the Committee for Human Rights, being the Croatian Helsinki Committee for Human Rights, a letter by Mr. Cicak. Did you know of Mr. Cicak and his involvement in these issues at that time or have you heard of his involvement in these matters?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I know Mr. Cicak personally. I didn't know, I don't remember, his involvement in the matter at the time --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is Mr. Cicak still involved with the Helsinki Committee in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, I'm not certain. I don't think so. Mr. Cicak is a public figure who was involved in various public activities either through his membership of various political parties, through his membership of various non-governmental organizations. I believe that he is a journalist and I don't know where else he works. I am not aware of this report. This is the first time I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, to look at Exhibit P 10548 in the same binder, 3, 10548.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Which is an article written in the Christian Science Monitor on the 6th of January 1994 titled: "Croatian conscripts tell of Bosnian duty." Now, do any of that -- excuse me. Do any of those documents refresh your memory further over the fact that in late 1993 at least, perhaps other times, and in early 1994, men in Croatia were being conscripted and sent to fight in Bosnia-Herzegovina against their will?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I do see these articles. They cannot and do not need to refresh my memory because I never had knowledge of such events described here. I cannot assert whether these events happened or not. If they did, then I can only say that this was a grave error. I didn't -- I wasn't aware of it at the time and I cannot tell you whether this is correct or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, sir. If I could ask you to next turn to P 10545, which again is in binder 3, 10545. This is an article from the New York Times dated the 24th of November, 2003, and you're referenced in the -- about halfway down the page you'll see some -- a statement attributed to you. "Miomir Zuzul, the former ambassador to the United States who is likely to be named foreign minister, said, 'Croatia will be led by a moderate centre-right government over the next four years.'" Next paragraph: "The victory for the Croatian Democratic Union follows an overhaul of its image, and a purge of the extremists, some of whom were implicated in war crimes committed during the 1991 to 1995 Balkan wars." As someone who was, as you've told us, was very involved in these events at the time and held very senior positions in the government back during that time-period, can you tell us who some of the extremists were that were purged from the party?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Croatian Democratic Union, as is well-known to those who follow the political events in Croatia, redefined itself in a way in 2000 and defined itself clearly as a centre-right political party quite open and prepared to cooperate with the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My question was more direct, sir. Can you tell the Judges while we have you here and the benefit of your knowledge, can you name some of the extremists who were purged from the party as a result of this overhaul. I'm talking about if you can give us names, please.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, quite a few of them left the party. I would not dare to name any names because I did not take part in the process and to thus categorize these people as extremists. All those who did not wish to accept the new policy of the HDZ as it was defined by the president of the party, Mr. Ivo Sanader, left the party, either lost the intra-party elections or were thrown out of the party. Quite a few of them left the party that way. Now, were all of them extremists, well, I certainly would not say that one --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... give us one names at least.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not see that my testimony should serve to define the positions of anyone, of any politician. Those who did not wish or feel that they were a part of that party anymore left the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You may or may not want to answer, I think you should, but that's my question to you. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: May I say something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think I can answer such a question because I was not in a -- I am not in a position to know what the political views of a particular person were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Prlic. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: A question was made but this is not quoting what Mr. Zuzul told in his interview. And this is for the third time he was asked about something he didn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I never said that he said it, but I did put it to him and as a senior government official and a member of this party that if that's true. If he says that that didn't happen, that this is not a true statement, that extremists were not purged from the party after -- between the war and the elections in 2003, then he can say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Witness, we have a text in front of us, and apparently you granted an interview to the New York Times. And you know that as well as I do when somebody says something the press will quote the words uttered by the interviewee, and here apparently some words are put into -- between inverted commas. I see, and it may be what Mr. Prlic was referring to, the purge of extremists and those involved in war crimes, those words are not presented as quotations. So this might lead to think that now it is the journalist drawing this conclusion based possibly on an off-the-record discussion you had with him or her but it's not being quoted between inverted commas. So what is it? Are these conclusions drawn by the journalist or does he report an off-the-record conversation you might have had with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. As one can glean from the text, this was not a conversation only with me but with several personalities from the Croatian political life and some of them are mentioned here. It is the journalist's statement that is reported here and not mine. Now, why did I not want to make such a statement directly? Because the change occurring in my political party, in the HDZ, occurred at the time while I was not in Croatia but in the United States of America. I welcomed the change and I publicly commended the work of Ivo Sanader. The fact that he won the election for the president of the HDZ against Mr. Pasalic is something that evidently shows that change did occur in that party. I welcomed the change and I still do. The HDZ was being reformed. Now, it is very difficult for me to answer the question as to who the extremists were because in such a way I would be attributing political views to an individual who perhaps did not hold those views, especially so when these extremists are placed in the context of war crimes. I really do not know who committed war crimes in the territory of Croatia or in any other territory of the former Yugoslavia, but as Mr. Prosecutor knows full well the government I was a member of was prepared in all the ways to cooperate with the Tribunal and with all the international organizations in order to ascertain the truth, that is, who it was who committed crimes and who did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, we'll come back to that topic in a few moments. Let me turn back to your -- the positions you held and your previous training. Based on what you've told us, sir, and based on a review of your CV that I've seen various places that's available, prior to 1991 -- prior to April of 1992, is it correct to say that -- had you had -- well, let me just ask you. Had you had any military training or experience prior to April or March 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prior to March or April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Prior to --

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I as a -- in fact, the majority of Croats, as the majority of the citizens of the then-Yugoslavia, I served my military service in the Yugoslav People's Army in 1982 for some ten months. I had the training that was compulsory for all the adult men at the time. I wouldn't say that I had had any special military training.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just in terms of reviewing your advanced degrees at least, you received a masters in social psychology in 1983 and a Ph.D. in psychology in 1987; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And at the time -- at the time that you were appointed or at least -- excuse me, let me -- at the time that the war broke out and fighting in 1991 and I believe you said you spent some time -- part time working in the Croatian army, at that time you were a professor of psychology at the University of Zagreb; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Sometime in early September 1991, I, together with a group of colleagues from the university, reported to the Croatian army as a volunteer. Prior to that I was a professor at the Croatian faculty in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just to be clear, when you say reported to the Croatian army to volunteer, were you offering your services in a civilian capacity or did you become a member of the Croatian army at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I became a member of the Croatian army; however, since we were all university professors we offered our professional knowledge, and that knowledge was not in the art of war but in the various fields that we were involved in in our day-time job.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you continue working at the same time at the university?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when it was that I formally left. In Croatia there is a law which to some extent differs to the law in other countries, that was still in the former Yugoslavia. If you leave your post at a university, for instance, because you have a certain duty to perform, then your job status with the university remains valid. So for all those years over which I was engaged on other duties, based on the labour law in Croatia my formal employment and my work booklet lay with the University of Zagreb. And I was even allowed to, to the extent I had time -- the spare time to do that, to even teach at the university. Some of my colleagues did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You said earlier in your testimony at page 27609 that this group of you that you've just described again in the last few moments set up a "department that dealt with psychological and informational aspects of the war." Is that something that either was or became known as the IPD administration?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that that's precisely it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And IPD stands for what, information propaganda?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Initially, IPD meant the information and psychological activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did that department or entity ever further evolve into some sort of intelligence service?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that the department ever evolved into an intelligence service. The department did evolve, but unless I'm mistaken, an intelligence service was already in existence before the department was set up and developed over time. I'm not sure how -- what the communication between the two was. I know that an intelligence service existed at the time when I was performing this other duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, at the risk of taking a bit of time, can you tell us exactly the nature of the work at the time of this psychological and information department? What were you actually doing? What services were being provided to the armed forces in that capacity?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived there and when we set it in motion, it was the early days of the department. As a psychology professor I was engaged in a large research project titled: Children in war. Through the project we tried to assist children, victims of war, by giving them psychological counselling, and a large number of experts were involved in that activity. Through my work there I realized that adults were in fact faced with many difficulties, persons who were refugees or who hailed from war-torn areas. I, together with some other psychologists, tried to develop some preventative measures aimed at countering the development of the post-traumatic disorder, the PTSD. The focus of our work was to counter psychological problems, and we looked at how the US army dealt with that during World War II --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... significant amount of time to give your answer to that, but let me move on, please. During your involvement with the Croatian armed forces, during that period in the early 1990s, did you raise -- did you ever rise to any particular rank or were you given any particular rank during that time-period?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I received a rank while I was in the Croatian army, the rank of a brigadier

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you give us any particular assistance as to, if you know, how that particular rank might fit into the rank hierarchy of a Western army in terms of -- where I -- in the United States, for example, a brigadier is typically referred to as a brigadier-general. Is that the same in Croatia or does it mean something different?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Croatia the rank of brigadier is somewhat lower than the brigadier-general but a bit higher than a colonel. The logic behind these ranks was the one that the US army developed during World War II when they included a number of professors, university professors, particularly psychologists in the army and the ranks coincided with their expertise, with their expert knowledge, rather than their military performance. And we followed the very same logic in developing these ranks in the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, moving forward to your positions as assistant minister of foreign affairs and then a few months later deputy minister of foreign affairs, based on your CV and what you've told us in your testimony, prior to that time you had no experience, you had no education or training or experience in diplomacy or foreign affairs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Around this same time-period can you tell us, and that is in, let's say 1992, during the time you became -- took up your post in the foreign affairs, what role or position did President Tudjman's son, Miroslav Tudjman, have in the Croatian government?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Miroslav Tudjman who was in that same group of university professors who volunteered to become members of the Croatian army and who participated in the setting up of the IPD department with me, I think that he stayed behind as a member of the army when I left it. If you're referring to the positions he held later on, I think that this happened a bit later after I had left the army that he transferred to the intelligence service of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At what point did he become the head of one of the national intelligence services of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unless I'm mistaken, it was at the very end of 1992. I'm not positive about it, but I believe it was the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And which particular intelligence service was this, because there may be several in the Croatian government at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a brief time I was appointed advisor for national security to President Tudjman, and there our task was through organizational cooperation to propose cooperation with other friendly states, that is -- or rather, in cooperation with other friendly states to make a proposal for the organization of intelligence services in Croatia. I didn't work on this long, but I did start working on this with Mr. Miro Tudjman and --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Zuzul, sorry to interrupt you. Perhaps you misunderstood or my question's mistranslated or I'm sure -- I'll take responsibility for any confusion. My question to you, you referred to Miroslav Tudjman taking up a position as head of an intelligence service at the end of 1992. My question was if you could simply identify that particular intelligence service. There is something -- there was after that time, it may have been at the time, there was an agency called the Croatian Information Service, HIS; there was the Security Information Service which I believe was part of the Ministry of Defence, SIS, perhaps there were others. So which of the intelligence services was Miroslav Tudjman the head of by the end of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what I was trying to say. To the best of my recollection, he became the head of the HIS, H-I-S, which was a newly established service based on what I was just trying to say, if my memory serves me well and I think it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then you referred to, I was going to ask you that next, you referred to an appointment as national security advisor to President Tudjman sometime during the period 1992/1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was sometime in the autumn of 1992. I don't recall the precise date, but, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And again, sir, prior to your appointment as assistant minister of defence -- excuse me, minister of foreign affairs in March 1992, had you had any training or involvement or previous experience other than your ten months of service in the JNA in 1992, anything that might be called national security?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: A translation problem that the very last sentence of yours, Mr. Scott, it says, anything that might be called national service, and you said security.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If it was my mistake, Your Honour, I apologise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: No, you said security and in the transcript it is service, so it should be replaced. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Prandler.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, could you answer my question. Did you have any prior training, experience, background in anything called national security?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, neither did the vast majority of Croats. I had no experience, to be quite frank. My service in the JNA is not something I would term experience in national security.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, I have to put to you that based on this review that we've conducted in the last few minutes, and I don't mean to offend you particularly but I do have to put to you this point, and that is based on what you've told us I see no, absolutely no previous experience, training, or qualification for these extremely senior positions in government that you found yourself in in 1992 and 1993. And is it fair to say, sir, that your principal qualification for those positions were being a close friend of Gojko Susak and a close friend of Miroslav Tudjman, the president's son?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course you have the right to any opinion you choose to adopt, but this is completely incorrect. At that time I was one of the youngest professors at Zagreb University. I was the youngest vice-dean of a faculty at the university. I was already a professor in the USA. In Croatian conditions, all these are major results. I dealt with aggressive behaviour --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... anything to do with military service or national security or diplomacy or foreign policy, it had absolutely nothing to do with those fields, sir.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: But when you put such a personal question to me, you should allow me to complete my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you look at the structure of the Croatian government, the other persons in the government, when I was deputy minister my immediate superior was Professor Dr. Zdenko Skrabalo, a professor of medicine who had even less experience than I did. He was succeeded by Dr. Mate Granic, a professor of medicine. When you look at who the Croatian ambassadors were, none of them, almost none of them had any previous experience in diplomacy. Why? Well, the reason is the following. Apart from a very small number of those who did have experience, no persons who had such experience chose to join the Croatian option, and this includes both -- both civil servants and the army. I became assistant minister of foreign affairs, and my task was to select staff members, and as a psychologist I had dealt with such issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time there were 35 people in the Croatian diplomatic service, only half of them --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... some minutes to go further with your question -- your answer, excuse me. Sir, isn't -- again, wasn't your primary qualification that you were President Tudjman's man, you were deeply loyal to President Tudjman, both at the time in 1992, 1993, 1994, and thereafter. You were the president's man, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not take that as an insult because had I not been loyal to those I worked with, I would not have done that job. I had many critical comments to make about President Tudjman, but I did accept him as the president of my country and as the man I worked with. Had I thought this was something opposed to my principles, I would have left the job. However, I find it completely unacceptable because I have held many positions in the international community. And certainly it was not my friendship with Miro Tudjman or anyone else or my loyalty to President Tudjman that got me there. That loyalty was understood as my doing my job honestly under difficult conditions and you can check that with your colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you -- I apologise to the interpreters. Let me ask you, please, to turn to Exhibit P 10401 in binder 3, P 10401, binder 3. Do you have it? Sir, this appears to be an interview that you gave or at least purports to be an interview that you gave on the 10th of December, 1992, titled at least in part or referenced here as: "Interview with Miomir Zuzul, deputy foreign minister of the Republic of Croatia." Now, if I can direct your attention to the middle of the second page, under -- there's a heading on the middle of that page that says: "I would refuse the position of prime minister ..." In the paragraph that follows, let me refer to that place and then put a question or two to you. "There are at least three reasons why people believe that Miomir Zuzul until recently 'only' professor and head of the department of developmental and child psychology in the school of philosophy at Zagreb University but today deputy foreign minister of the Republic of Croatia and the president's national security adviser, is one of the most powerful and promising people in Croatian politics. He is from Imok, and they say that that lobby is fairly strong. It is said that Miomir Zuzul is 'Susak's man' and the power of the defence minister is well-known. Aside from that, he is a personal friend of the president's son. A third reason has to do with his job. People believe that the very fact that someone is involved in the organization of the intelligence service, in this case within the foreign affairs sector, is already sufficient reason for personal political power." Now, do you recall that, I assume, you gave an interview back in 1992, I think probably if most people give an interview and it comes out in the press, I guess we're all proud enough or what have you that we want to read the interview. Do you remember those words being written about you in December of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now it is coming back to me when I see this interview, but as we can see these are words written by a journalist. Had you wanted to read the next sentence, which we can all read now, in the next sentence it says that even then I denied what the journalist was saying, the fact that this journalist wrote that. Had it been correct, I would really have become prime minister within a few months or the minister of foreign affairs because both those posts were filled with new people a few months later. I became an ambassador of the Republic of Croatia. I'm not complaining about that. It was an honour and I was proud of it, but it shows that what the journalist thought at that point in time was not -- did not reflect reality in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I refer you further down the page where the -- statements are attributed to you directly, questions are -- excuse me, questions are put to you by the interviewer and then you'll see in brackets (Zuzul) and then it starts out: "Taken individually ..." I'm just giving you that as a landmark. If you go to the next paragraph which is still attributed to you speaking, it says this: "Susak? I'm a friend of his, I hope, but I have not known him long either. Watching him through the war and through politics I recognise that this is a man worthy of esteem. I belong to no one, not even to Susak, but I acknowledge that we are working along the same political line, that is, we have a similar political option which in the final analysis is not Susak's but the president's. In that sense, both Susak and I are the president's men but he is the closer and stronger one." Is that the statement that you gave to the interviewer in December 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, that's the statement I gave then and I would not change it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Staying on the topic of intelligence services or coming back to that again, which has been mentioned several times in the last few minutes. Did you ever have any dealings or have dealings with a man involved in intelligence named Markica Rebic?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew Mr. Rebic well. He comes from the same town I come from. For a while we both worked together in the secondary school in Imotski. However, when he became involved in intelligence we had very little contact and our personal contact, private contact, ceased as early as the early [as interpreted] 1990s.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] As the mid-1990s, I said. There is mistake in translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say "mid-1990s," sir, can you help us a bit more with that. Mid-1990s could be, I suppose, anything from 1993 to 1998. Can you help us?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I became the ambassador to Geneva, Mr. Rebic, to the best of my recollection, was not yet involved in intelligence work. When he did join the intelligence service, I was already a diplomat. And in the nature of our work we didn't have a lot of contact. Privately, our contacts grew less because I gained the impression that there was a certain circle of people within the then-HDZ and within the institutions which did not gladly accept me. When you have such an impression about someone you have known for years, whether your impression is correct or not, your relations cool and that's what happened between me and Mr. Rebic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Back a few months ago in October of 2007 when a verdict was issued by this institution in the so-called Vukovar case, you're reported by the Croatian news service HINA as saying that -- you were very critical of the verdict. You say you hoped it was a mistake and you said that the ICTY verdict "has scandalised the whole civilised world." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can we get the -- where this comes from. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: A HINA report on the 1st of October, 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Which document is it on?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's not an exhibit, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, if it is not an exhibit I would object.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't have to put an exhibit to the witness, Mr. Karnavas, and you know that. That is my basis for asking the question, you do not have to put every document to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I beg to differ. I think it's professional courtesy to at least give counsel the opportunity to see if whether you're quoting the document correctly. I will take it that you're bona fides, but I don't think that you should presume that I should have to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall making that statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it would be -- show courtesy to show the witness that article.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, are you denying that you made such a statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one moment. Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, now that this is being discussed there was several documents previously which were in English only. Mr. Prlic responded but we were unable to participate to understand. So could we, the accused, be provided with the documents in a language we understand? There were several documents in English only. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, this report by HINA, you don't have it, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Not in the courtroom, sir, and I strongly in the most uncertain terms -- most certain terms, excuse me, I disagree with counsel. We do our investigation, we read a lot of documentation. I prepare questions. I do not have to show every document on which I base a question to the witness. The witness can tell us very easily, if he says he never gave such an interview or made such a statement, he can tell us that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, is it -- are you telling us that you don't recall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness may answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you -- [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, I don't know why you are putting in my mouth what I want to say or don't want to say. I want to answer every question, and if I don't know the answer I will say I don't know. There's no need for you to answer in my stead. I did make a statement, and like most people in Croatia I do think it was a bad decision. I don't know whether the statement was made in the precise words you quoted because I don't see it before me, but in investigating me and my life you must have seen that I'm a person who held certain principles throughout, who from 1993 to this day have supported the work of this Tribunal, not only as a Croat but also as a member of the international community. And I think I have done quite a lot and that's how I came to be here. So when I thought that a decision had been made which was not just, in view of what had happened, I said so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I didn't put any words in your mouth. I was asking a question, I may have had some arguments with counsel, but I never put words in your mouth except to ask you if you were critical of that judgement. Now, you said you were and I didn't say there was anything wrong with that. Of course you're entitled to your opinion, but I simply wanted to just establish that by way of background. Further on that, sir, and based on what you just told us about your attitude toward the Tribunal, can we agree, sir, that this Tribunal can only do its work and judgements can only be issued, good or bad, based upon the evidence and information that is gathered and put before this Tribunal, much of which must come from the states of the former Yugoslavia. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, completely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you were instrumental, were you not, in the hiring of a Washington DC attorney named David Rivkin to represent the Republic of Croatia in the 1990s before this Tribunal; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the way you formulated it. When I was appointed to the post of ambassador in Washington, Mr. Rivkin was already working for the Croatian Embassy and the Republic of Croatia. I met him, I was introduced to him as somebody who had already been recruited by Minister Granic, if I'm not wrong, and this had happened at least half a year before I arrived. I was introduced to Mr. Rivkin, I had good cooperation with him. I thought then, as I do now, that he did a good job for the Republic of Croatia, but my communication with him was almost exclusively concerning his work as a lobbyist for the Republic of Croatia in Washington and not concerning his representing Croatia before the Tribunal. This was never organized through the Embassy of the Republic of Croatia in Washington.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may very briefly, it's evident that my learned friend is going somewhere with this. In any case, the last two questions, especially the last one concerning Mr. Rivkin, is difficult to evaluate as to relevance. What can the witness's possible contact with an American attorney-at-law while he was an ambassador in Washington, all of which occurred after all the events in the indictment, all of this has to be shown to be relevant, otherwise it's a pure waste of time. So the relevance has to be established. We sense where this might be going and then it's irrelevant. So please let this be established first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, if you asked that question you probably had a goal. I must admit that I'm a little lost. I can't see precisely what you're aiming at, but please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is the objection overruled, Your Honour, because there's a question on relevance. Is Mr. Rivkin here now being tried for errors and omissions --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's not the standard of relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that the Prosecutor must have a goal, an aim, so I asked him to proceed in order to see what his aim is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. I misunderstood you, Mr. President. I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you, sir, to turn to Exhibit P 10544, which will be found in the binder 3. You have that, sir. This is an article in the Washington Post dated the 1st of July, 2000. I would like to refer you to the -- well, let's start at the top. It says: "Top Croatian ministers looked to a Washington attorney for advice in recent years as they weighed demands from the International War Crimes Tribunal for information about alleged atrocities committed by Croatian troops in the 1991 to 1995 Bosnian war" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, Mr. Kovacic wants to intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it has been established before this Tribunal that the accused have the right to see exhibits in a language they understand. This is not the first document in this binder which we do not have in Croatian. I propose that for this reason the use of this document be prevented, and of any document in future which is not translated into Croatian, as was every document that the Defence could not use if it had not been translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, the accused must have the document in their own language; however, sometimes documents are shown in B/C/S, we don't have any translation available. The document is then placed on the ELMO, we read out the relevant paragraph, and then it is up to the interpreters to translate the document for everybody's benefit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't mean to -- just one last intervention on this, on the grounds of relevancy. As far as I'm aware, there have been no accusations or charges against Mr. Rivkin with the bar association concerning any illegal activity or unprofessional activity that he conducted, that's number one, on behalf of Croatia or in his private practice. Number two, as you may know, an attorney of the United States who represents a foreign government has to -- has to get clearance in that, in those affairs. So it's very well-known by the United States Government that Mr. Rivkin was representing another country because they have to be registered as such if they're going to be doing any lobbying work. I really fail to see on what grounds we're going into Mr. Rivkin's activities. If he gave bad advice to a client, shame on him, they should take him before the DC bar association. But what does this have to do with Mr. Zuzul, what does it have to do with the case, what does it have to do with the indictment? I would beg -- demand from Mr. Scott his basis as opposed to showing the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, in order to save time you asked for the additional time, you were granted additional time. What did you want to establish by mentioning Mr. Rivkin? As far as I'm concerned, it's the first time that I hear about this gentleman.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, in order to do that we would have to excuse the witness and go into private session. I do not have to lay out the rationale and goals of my cross-examination in front of the very witness who's being examined. So if you would like to do that, if you would like to excuse the witness and go private session, I would be happy to address it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, I would like to draw your attention to the following. The Prosecution advanced the suggestion that they just advanced; however, the Prosecution in another case before this Tribunal had a position that was quite the opposite to this one and in that case when the Judges asked the Defence to lay the foundation for their question the Prosecution opposed the request that the witness leave the courtroom. So I'm quite surprised that the Prosecution should now be asking that the witness be requested to leave the courtroom, so there must be a hidden agenda there; I'm sure of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, which case did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was in the Kordic/Cerkez case, and by happenstance we were the counsel in that case, and I must say that the Presiding Judge in that case was in the habit of asking us whenever such a line of questioning was embarked upon, and of course the Presiding Judge, or rather, the Prosecutor could not know where this was heading, and of course the Presiding Judge would then ask us where we were going with our questions and we had to respond and we -- it was oftentime asked that the witnesses leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, what are you getting at? What is your purpose in the interest of time?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I disagree with counsel. I don't pretend, I'm not going to stand up and pretend to know the particular circumstances on that prior occasion, if that happened or not. It may have been for perfectly good reasons, I don't know. But I stand by the position that I'm cross-examining this witness, I want to put questions to this witness, and I do not have to lay out my plan of questioning in front of the witness before I put my questions to him. So I would be happy to talk to the Chamber, I would be very happy to talk to the Chamber, but not in the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall confer with my fellow Judges to see whether the witness is to leave the courtroom or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I just say before you deliver your ruling, as a matter of principle, I think it must be said that my learned friend Mr. Scott's proposition is quite correct. I don't see any problem at all with excusing the witness. It can't be right that a witness be forewarned as to a line of cross-examination. Of course that's another matter for the Court to know relevance. So I would commend my learned friend's proposition as being quite sensible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is what we're going to do. Witness, anyway, we were about to have a break. You're going to be excused out of the courtroom. Then we'll have a break, and as soon as you've left the courtroom Mr. Scott is going to tell us about his purpose. So please follow the usher witness and you can start your 20-minute break -- well, it will be a little longer for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, very quickly before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in -- again, I would ask to please go into private session because I think members of Mr. Zuzul's family are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, yes, you're right. Let's move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Please proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Zuzul, I think at one point we left off and I had directed your attention to -- yes, I'm sure I did, P 10544, and I do acknowledge to counsel, apparently we're not able to get translation of this particular in time. If we can have the English version brought up in e-court, I will ask for the interpreters' assistance. In fairness, Mr. Zuzul, I understand that you're quite fluent -- if I may say so, excellent speaker and I'm sure read excellent English. This article starts off -- we read the part before and then it goes on second paragraph to say: "Croatia's foreign minister privately urged the government to comply in full. But attorney David B. Rivkin Jr., at the time a partner in the law form Hunton & Williams, said at one point that cooperating would be the 'worst option' and urged the ministers instead to pursue diversionary legal tactics, according to records of government deliberations made available here." I'm pausing for the benefit of the interpreters. "Rivkin, whose view won the day, said his view [sic] was to present an aggressive defence of wartime actions by the Croatian government, then headed by President Franjo Tudjman, and help the government fend off the demands." Then it goes on in the next paragraph just to further finish on this particular aspect. "The new government has declared it wants to cooperate with the Tribunal, denounced Rivkin's legal strategies ..." Now, just to pause there for a minute, sir, this is indeed, however, the same David Rivkin that, then, you further involved with the Croatian government in terms of, I think you said, lobbying work in Washington DC; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor, I did not involve him. He had already been recruited to lobby in 1995, whereas I was appointed ambassador in 1996. As I said, I cooperated with him and I have to be sincere and say that I cooperated with him well but on work in Washington.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. My understanding is that at least as part of the work being performed by Mr. Rivkin he was hired in 1996 at your suggestion and with the approval of Franjo Tudjman; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what part of his work you are referring to. He was recruited to work for the Croatian state in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if I can direct your attention to Exhibit P 10542, which is again in the last binder, binder 3, P 10542. This is an article in a publication called Newsday, Washington bureau, dated the 25th of July, 1997, in which you are one of the persons featured, being quoted and referred to in the text of the article. Toward the bottom half of the page there is this paragraph just to set the context here. It says: "The Pentagon official" being referenced, "said Croatia 'should do more to bring ethnic Croat indictees before the Hague Tribunal.' The official said that Croatian President Franjo Tudjman can 'make things happen' if he seriously wants them to." Then it goes back and makes a statement apparently attributed to you: "The Croatian envoy also said his government will resist subpoenas handed down by the Tribunal for internal documents connecting Tudjman and his aides with the war waged in Bosnia by Bosnian Croats." Now, do you recall taking the position, and in fact announcing to this reporter that the Croatian government would resist turning over documents to the Tribunal in connection with Tudjman's involvement in the war in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall and I cannot confirm whether or not I said this or how I said it. It is correct, however, that the official policy of the Croatian government at the time was not to hand over documents as I understand it concerning events in Croatia, not events in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I was merely implementing the official policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I see. In fact, on that official policy if I can direct your attention to Exhibit P 10556, also in the third binder -- oh, I'm sorry. Are the interpreters -- excuse me, sorry. There is an interpretation of this document. Sorry, Ms. Winner is trying to help me out and doing a good job of it. Sir, if you will look now at this exhibit, P 10556, this is a report from Markica Rebic dated the 4th of June, 1998, to the president of the Republic of Croatia, Dr. Franjo Tudjman. And for current purposes I would like to direct your attention, please, first of all, to page 28 of this report in the English version so that the courtroom can have the fuller understanding of what this document is about. On page 28, sir, in paragraph number 4 provides us with this information: "In 1996, the HIS," and this was the intelligence agency that you identified earlier today as the one that became headed by Miroslav Tudjman at the end of 1992, "the HIS was assigned as the main protagonist responsible for carrying out Operation The Hague on the level of the Croatian government. This service corresponded to the HIS, that is, the SIS in the department -- department of defence, I believe, OZRH, Republic of Croatia, in all important aspects of authority." Going on to paragraph -- excuse me, on page 20 -- going back to page 20, please, with that connection involved -- in mind. At the top of page 20 this is reported to Franjo Tudjman by the intelligence service. "On the basis of ICTY documents, which this Service has acquired through intelligence methods and from reliable sources which have so far proved to be correct, we propose that the ultimate objective of the ICTY Prosecution is to link all indictments against Croats (Republic of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina) attributing responsibility to the top leadership, and the most prominent members of the RH leadership, including the President of the Republic of Croatia." Below that the Chamber may see that the reports about certain testimony given at the Tribunal. On page 34, top of page 34 numbered 4: "The defence strategy shall rest on the crucial position of non-involvement of the Republic of Croatia in the Muslim-Croat war in Central Bosnia (the legal question of 'an international armed conflict') ..." And then as to Operation Storm, Oluja, the separate issue of the ICTY's alleged lack of jurisdiction, and that's what is become known as the Gotovina case. Now, in that particular regard in connection with documents, sir, and in connection with what you said implementing official policy to resist turning over documents, in that context if I can next direct your attention, please, to page 23 of the same report, top of page 23: "When HVO archives became a serious problem in the course of preparation of General Blaskic's defence, with respect to the substance of the subpoena and ICTY's requests involving HVO officials, this Service, in cooperation with the HIS, took action and measures to protect the HVO archives." Now, sir, you said a few moments ago that you understood that you were implementing official policy in resisting the production of documents. Did you understand that policy to be consistent with what is stated in this document -- this report that I just put in front of you, is that the policy that you were implementing?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never seen this document before and I was not aware of its contents or the policy it refers to. It's quite difficult to me to draw conclusions from this particular viewpoint. There's a lot here I would not agree with, but I never received instructions couched in the terms presented here. It's correct that the policy which I knew of as an ambassador and which I tried to justify as best I could was that at that time the government considered that the Tribunal was -- did not have jurisdiction concerning the events of -- following Operation Storm and during Operation Storm. Whether there was a justified position or not, I -- that was the position. I tried to expound to my collocutors and some agreed with it and some did not. I am not sure, as regards other matters, that the position was what is represented in this document. I know that my instructions were always that we would, in fact, cooperate fully with the Tribunal as regards Bosnia-Herzegovina. And from the outset Croatia supported the work of the Tribunal, not -- we did not only pay lip service to that some of us but we actually supported the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we can go back, please, to P 10544, the Washington Post article, and there again if we put it on the e-court on this document we'll need the assistance of the interpreters, please. In the second page of that article toward the bottom of the page there is a paragraph that starts -- yes, it's on the screen now. "Based on what Rivkin says were false assurances by officials in the Tudjman government, he said that Hunton & Williams erroneously claimed in legal filings that it had fully complied with Tribunal demands for all documents related to the Ahmici atrocity." And I'll note that that has nothing to do with Operation Storm. "Shortly after taking office, however, the new government revealed that it had uncovered several intelligence agency files that not only named some of the Croatian militia members responsible for the slayings, but also revealed that Tudjman's government provided false identities and paid for homes where the men could hide from Tribunal arrest warrants in a scenic village on the Adriatic coast." Now, sir, did it ever come to your attention that at around the time that you were saying it was the official policy not to produce documents, that in fact subsequent to that these additional documents became known and ultimately were turned over to the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, I didn't quite understand your question. The official policy that all the documents were handed over -- may I read this in English? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time with respect to quite a lot of the things you are mentioning now, I was not aware of them and I don't know what is and what is not correct. If you as the Prosecutor of this institution or if this institution says that not all the documents which was subsequently handed over were handed over, then I believe you because I believe this institution far more than I believe Jeffrey Smith the journalist who wrote this article and whom I know personally. As regards your previous question, who were the extremists among the Croats, one name I can give you is Jeffrey Smith. I know of some other articles he wrote where he wrote all sorts of things starting from certain political positions. Having said that, I am not saying that what you say is not true. I do not know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I note that when it comes to talking about Mr. Jeffrey Smith, a person -- non-Croat person not in Zagreb, you're suddenly quite capable and willing to identify him as one of the extremists that you wouldn't tell us about before. What is it about Mr. Smith that makes you willing to identify him but not any of the others?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Smith is an American, if he's the person I'm thinking of, and I assume he is, an American of Croatian origin, close to a circle of Croats who hold relatively extreme political positions with whom, neither as an ambassador nor later on as a minister or politician, I never had close relations with them because they thought Croatian policy should be different from what it was. Of course they had the right to their opinion, and he expressed this opinion, if it's the same Jeffrey Smith, in several articles in which inter alia, if I remember correctly, he fiercely attacked the government I was part of for cooperating with the Tribunal in another case, using different arguments but starting from the starting point of a group which exists among Croats in America and I believe elsewhere. That's why I wanted to mention him. I'm not even saying it's the same Jeffrey Smith, but I assume it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we can go forward to another aspect of the report from Mr. Rebic that was actually then touched on in part of the Washington Post article that I just referred to and that is the protection -- the giving of false identities and protection of men or hiding on the Adriatic coast. If I can refer you back again to page 23 of Exhibit P 10556. Under the paragraph about the HVO archives is this paragraph, and we do have a translation of this. "This service established through counter-intelligence methods the existence of seven other secret indictments against Croats in Central Bosnia. On several occasions, it forwarded timely information" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Scott, I wonder which page?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Page 23. I apologise, Judge Prandler. Page 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: "On several occasions it forwarded timely information on the intention of SFOR members to arrest the individuals charged in secret indictments, and to that end measures were taken to hide and protect them. We are providing direct protection to four individuals from Central Bosnia who are subject to secret indictments; the HVO SIS is protecting one individual, while the remaining two persons were informed on time of their possible arrest." Now, do you recall having any information at the time, sir, that one of the persons being protected at this time, in 1996, was Ivica Rajic?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have any information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I direct your attention, please, to Exhibit P 10539 in the third binder, P 10539. Sir, this is a letter, again from you, in fact, to the Washington Post, published a letter to the editor, on 11 November 1996 which you were apparently responding to certain -- an article written concerning Mr. Ivica Rajic. We'll put that on the ELMO, please, we made need the assistance of the interpreters, please. You refer to in the second paragraph: "In his article, Mr. Dobbs wrote that Ivica Rajic, who is wanted by the United Nations War Crimes Tribunal was 'reportedly seen in a state-owned hotel' in Split. This report apparently drawn from a report appearing in the Croatian weekly Globus, is incorrect." At the end of the paragraph: "Contrary to the media assertions, the current movement or residence of Rajic remain unknown to Croatian authorities." And I note the date of this -- your letter to the Washington Post being 11 November 1996. Do you remember sending that letter to the Washington Post, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now that I see the letter, yes, I sent the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What kind of inquiries did you make of the Croatian government prior to sending your letter to determine whether, in fact, your government knew where Mr. Rajic was or not?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, as you are well aware I was a Croatian ambassador at the time. Any ambassador may seek instructions and this is what they often do, but no ambassador may conduct an inquiry into finding out whether the information he received from the government or not. Evidently, the Croatian government did -- was not able to know what was correct here or not. I received information from the Croatian government, on the basis of which I drafted the letter. Was I supposed to mistrust the information I received from the Croatian government? Was it true? I don't know. As I may have said, I hold the author of this article, Mr. Michael Dobbs in high esteem, he's a very good journalist and I can even say he's a very good friend. I wrote a response on the basis of the information I received from my very own government. I don't think any other ambassador would have done something different.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may be allowed one intervention that might help clear up the matter, I personally know a great deal about this issue. I would like to clarify one point. This particular paragraph says: "The current movement or residence of Rajic remain unknown." And at the time the letter was drafted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Will you take an oath? It seems to me that you are testifying now, Ms. Alaburic?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You're testifying without an oath?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I appeal to you to hear me out. You will see that I'm not making a statement of any sort; I'm merely drawing your attention to what is different in this paragraph and what the Prosecutor has to tie up with. This article was published in the Globus weekly at some point in time, it also says that a photograph was published of a man who was supposed to be Rajic but was not. It was a hotel staff. And then there follows this sentence: "... the current movement ... of Mr. Rajic ..." is such and such. The time at which this statement was given to the editorial office does not coincide with the publishing of the Globus article, so that both the Globus article and this particular letter could have been true. I'm merely trying to point out that these refer to two different time-periods. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you will next direct your attention, please, to Exhibit P 10546, P 10546, in binder 3. In a nutshell, sir, this is a letter from the Republic of Croatia, Ministry of Defence, dated the 17th of June, 1996, in which Ivica Rajic's employment with the minister of defence is extended. If you look under "Decision" at the first paragraph above "Statement of reasons." "The service is being extended for a duration of six months to carry out the same job duties starting on 30 December 1994 ..." continuing on. This is dated the 17th of June, 1996, if my calculations are correct, six months would have extended to at least the 17th of December, 1996. So, sir, were you aware that when you reported that the Croatian government did not know of Mr. Rajic's whereabouts or movements, that at that very time he was employed and paid by the Croatian Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I wasn't aware of that and I don't know how I could have been aware of that as an ambassador. I only knew what my government informed me of. Whether somebody inside the system was aware of that I don't know and I cannot testify to that. But most certainly, had I known that this was not correct, I would not have written a letter such as this one because the crucial sentence in the entire letter is at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I next want to turn to the topic of Mr. Ivo Komsic again, whose name has come up several times in your testimony. You had a number of contacts with Mr. Komsic in the negotiations, the peace negotiations, in the latter part of 1993, early part of 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a number of contacts with -- with others I even had more contacts so I can't define the significance of that, but most definitely I contacted Mr. Komsic and he contacted me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I believe in your testimony on direct examination in reference to the joint -- the document that was put before you at the time was a joint declaration by Tudjman and Izetbegovic on the 14th of September, 1993, and that was Exhibit 1D, if I'm not mistaken, 1D 01535, we're not -- just for the purposes of the record. I'm not going to open it. But the persons who signed that document on the -- the persons who signed that document, among others, included Mr. Komsic and I believe -- and yourself on 14th of September, 1993. And I believe you testified at page 27788 that the persons who signed that document were among those persons having the greatest political influence or impact in Bosnia-Herzegovina around that time. Do you remember giving that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what it was that I exactly said. I did say that the document was signed the way you described it. Perhaps I may have referred to the greatest political influence, but I certainly did not have Mr. Komsic in mind. I did say, and I can repeat it, that Mr. Komsic helped bring the agreement about. I said before, and I believe I repeated it today, that at the meeting preceding this one there was Ambassador Biscevic and I on the one side, Mr. Silajdzic and Mr. Komsic on the other side. I also said in my earlier evidence that President Tudjman had certain reservations vis-a-vis the possibility of Mr. Komsic representing the other side. After a lengthy conversation with him, and if I can put it that way, my comments that this was the express wish of the Muslim side and if this was the way in which we would reach an agreement, it would be a good idea to agree to Mr. Komsic. President Tudjman responded to that by saying, Very well, but then Mr. Biscevic will be accompanying you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I think if you will remember back to a transcript that we were looking at earlier, presidential transcript on record that we were looking at earlier today and I believe at the end of the day yesterday, it was a record for the 13th of February, 1994, and in that transcript you made -- you and others made reference to the involvement of Mr. Komsic in the negotiations in Geneva at that time. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the transcript from the meeting of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes -- no, no, the Presidency of Croatia. The one that you reported about and you gave -- made certain statements that the ICFY was on its deathbed and you're reporting about the Washington developments and it was a transcript of that meeting. I don't think in the interests of time we need to pull out the transcript. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes? All right. And --
